input:
This review examines the cost of a regional delivery route, drawing on carrier invoices for the last 12 months in order to establish what the route has actually cost over a full year of operation. The headline result is that the annual transport cost is $155k, a figure that reflects the route exactly as it was operated during the period in question.

The route itself runs 163 km per trip at $1.8 per km, which corresponds to a derived cost of $293.4 per trip, and over the year as a whole the route accumulated a total of 527 trips per year. It is important to appreciate how this cost is structured: because the distance travelled on each trip is essentially fixed by the geography of the route, and because the rate per kilometre is set by the arrangement with the carrier, the annual cost is driven above all by the number of trips that are made. Another point that deserves emphasis is that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the $155k figure captures the full cost of operating the route, including those occasions on which a vehicle travelled without a load, rather than the cost of the loaded deliveries considered in isolation.

There are, inevitably, some limitations to what can be concluded from this analysis. The invoices relate to the route as a whole, so it is not possible to break the cost down by individual legs or by individual stops, nor to judge which of the trips were strictly necessary. Furthermore, the figures cover a single year, so they cannot reveal how the cost might change in a year with a different pattern of demand. Nevertheless, the review establishes the annual transport cost at $155k on a clearly stated basis, and it suggests that attention should be directed towards the trip count as the principal lever available for reducing it.
target:
Annual transport cost on the regional delivery route is $155k. The figure is built from carrier invoices for the last 12 months and covers every trip the route ran in that period, loaded and empty.

The route runs 163 km per trip at $1.8 per km, a derived cost of $293.4 per trip, and ran 527 trips per year. Cost therefore scales with trip count before it scales with anything else: the per-kilometre rate is fixed by the carrier arrangement recorded in the invoices, and the distance is fixed by the route, so the annual figure moves when the number of trips moves. Empty running is included in the trip count. The $155k is consequently the cost of the route as operated, not the cost of the loaded deliveries alone, and a comparison that strips out empty running would produce a lower figure on a different basis.

The review prices what the carrier charged, and the invoices are the whole of its evidence: no separate record of mileage, load, or waiting time stands behind the annual figure, so no part of it can be re-based from within the review itself. Two limits govern the use of the figure. The invoices price the route as a whole, so the review cannot separate the cost of individual legs or stops, and it cannot say which trips were necessary. The record also covers one year only, so it shows the cost at the trip count and rate of that year and nothing about either quantity in another year. On its stated basis the annual transport cost stands at $155k, and any saving case has to be argued from the trip count, because that is the term the operation controls.
